description: SELENE is a one-person project for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Using NASA's LOLA terrain data, JPL Horizons, and SPICE, SELENE transforms complex lunar science into an interactive platform to compare landing sites, explore solar illumination, visualize Sun and Earth positions, and assess potential communication windows. Our mission is to make lunar exploration more accessible, intuitive, and scientifically transparent.
summary:
Where should humanity land on the Moon, and when will conditions be favorable?

SELENE is an interactive lunar exploration platform that transforms NASA data into actionable insights for evaluating potential landing sites near the Moon's south pole. By combining NASA's LOLA terrain measurements, JPL Horizons ephemerides, and SPICE-based Deep Space Network geometry, SELENE helps users explore three critical challenges of lunar operations: sunlight availability, Earth visibility, and potential communication windows.

Through an interactive lunar globe, local horizon simulations, time-based analysis, and side-by-side comparisons of nine candidate locations, users can discover how terrain and celestial motion shape opportunities for lunar exploration.

Designed for accessibility and scientific transparency, SELENE makes complex lunar environmental data easier to understand, compare, and explore—bringing the challenges of future Moon missions closer to everyone.
details:
SELENE — Lunar South Pole Navigator

Exploring where sunlight, terrain, and Earth connectivity meet on the Moon.

The Challenge: Finding the Right Place at the Right Time

The Moon's south pole is one of the most promising regions for future lunar exploration, but it also presents some of the most challenging environmental conditions.

Unlike Earth, where the Sun generally rises high above the horizon, sunlight near the lunar poles often arrives at extremely low angles. Even relatively small terrain features can cast long shadows, creating dramatic differences in illumination between nearby locations.

These conditions have direct implications for solar-powered equipment, surface exploration, and mission planning. Communication with Earth introduces another challenge: crater walls, elevated terrain, and the relative motion of celestial bodies can obstruct direct line-of-sight connections.

A location that receives sunlight may not simultaneously have a clear communication path to Earth. Another location might offer better visibility but experience longer periods of darkness.

This raises a fundamental question:

How can we compare potential lunar landing sites while accounting for sunlight, terrain, and communication conditions together?

Our Solution: Introducing SELENE

SELENE is an interactive lunar exploration platform that transforms NASA scientific data into an accessible environment for comparing potential landing locations near the Moon's south pole.

Rather than treating illumination, topography, and Earth connectivity as separate problems, SELENE brings them together into a unified experience.

Users can select two candidate locations, explore their surrounding terrain, examine the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth, and compare potential communication opportunities over time.

The platform combines a visual lunar globe with quantitative analysis, allowing users to move between an intuitive understanding of the Moon's geography and measurable environmental indicators.

SELENE is designed to help users answer three essential questions:

  1. Sunlight: Is any meaningful portion of the Sun visible above the local terrain horizon?
  2. Earth visibility: Is the center of Earth above the local horizon?
  3. Communication: Is a geometric line of sight potentially available to at least one of NASA's three modeled Deep Space Network antennas?

By analyzing these conditions together, SELENE helps reveal how lunar terrain and celestial geometry shape the opportunities and constraints of surface exploration.

How SELENE Works

1. Explore Nine Lunar South Pole Locations

SELENE provides an interactive lunar globe displaying nine candidate locations associated with regions considered for NASA's Artemis III mission.

Each location is represented by a specific research-based coordinate, allowing the platform to analyze actual geographic points rather than treating entire candidate regions as uniform environments.

Users can rotate the Moon, inspect site markers, and select two distinct locations for comparison.

A synchronized minimap helps maintain spatial orientation during exploration.

2. Understand the Local Horizon

The surrounding terrain determines whether the Sun or Earth is visible from a particular location.

SELENE generates local horizon profiles using elevation measurements from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA).

The horizon visualization displays terrain elevation by azimuth and overlays the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth at the selected time.

An interactive local terrain view provides additional spatial context, helping users understand how nearby topography influences visibility.

3. Investigate Solar Illumination

SELENE combines local terrain horizons with astronomical positions obtained from NASA/JPL Horizons.

Instead of treating sunlight as a simple visible-or-hidden condition, the system estimates how much of the apparent solar disk clears the local horizon.

This enables users to examine partial solar visibility and compare illumination conditions between locations.

The application also calculates the proportion of hourly samples in which the Sun meets its visibility threshold during a selected comparison period.

These results help illustrate potential solar-energy opportunities, although they do not represent electrical power generation or complete energy-system performance.

4. Explore Direct-to-Earth Communication Opportunities

Communication is essential for transmitting scientific data, receiving instructions, and coordinating lunar surface activities.

SELENE evaluates potential geometric visibility involving three NASA Deep Space Network stations:

  • Goldstone DSS-14, United States.
  • Canberra DSS-43, Australia.
  • Madrid DSS-63, Spain.

Using NAIF/SPICE geometry, the platform examines whether a station has a potential line of sight to the lunar location, considering the local terrain horizon and a minimum Earth-station elevation of six degrees.

Users can identify periods when communication geometry is favorable and examine how those opportunities overlap with sunlight availability.

These are geometric visibility estimates, not confirmed antenna availability or operational communication schedules.

5. Travel Through Lunar Time

Environmental conditions on the Moon change over time.

SELENE includes an interactive timeline that allows users to move through the simulation, play time forward at different speeds, and compare seven-, fourteen-, or twenty-eight-day periods.

The current scientific dataset covers January 15 through February 13, 2027 (UTC), with hourly samples used for quantitative calculations.

Users can investigate how solar illumination, Earth visibility, and potential communication conditions evolve throughout the selected period.

6. Compare Locations and Identify Overlapping Opportunities

One of SELENE's central capabilities is its side-by-side comparison system.

Users can compare two candidate locations using consistent indicators, including solar visibility, Earth visibility, potential DSN connectivity, and the periods when favorable conditions occur simultaneously.

An availability timeline displays the hourly environmental states and their overlap.
